metadata.title: Great House Farm: A Chronicle of Dispossession
metadata.subtitle: Complete Screenplay - Dialogue Only Format
metadata.notes: Timeline corrected against verified legal record: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 (Court of Appeal, Dillon LJ, 31 Jul 1987). Key corrections: adverse possession from Feb 1955 (last rent ~1953); first possession order 11 Dec 1962; 1974 licence letters by BP Pension Trust; Mary Williams died 1983; QBD judgment Hollis J 24 Jul 1986; CA judgment NOT House of Lords.

scenes.narration: Robert Fitzhamon grants the lordship of Llandough to the Walsche family, establishing feudal control of the area that includes the future Great House Farm.

dialogue.speaker: ROBERT FITZHAMON
dialogue.line: I grant Walsche the Llandough lordship to manage, tax and defend.

dialogue.speaker: LORD WALSCHE
dialogue.line: We now hold Llandough and its revenues under Fitzhamon's grant.

scenes.narration: A substantial stone residence, Tŷ Mawr ('Great House'), is constructed beside St Dochdwy's church at Llandough as a manorial house, later known as Great House Farm.

dialogue.speaker: MASTER MASON
dialogue.line: We're building a new stone manorial house beside St Dochdwy's.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL FARMER
dialogue.line: Local lord's new stone house next to the parish church. Right ho!

scenes.narration: Tewkesbury Abbey and the Prior of Cardiff hold Great House and its lands, taking tithes and agricultural income from Llandough for over three centuries.

dialogue.speaker: ABBOT'S STEWARD
dialogue.line: Llandough's produce and tithes are entered as revenue for the abbey.

dialogue.speaker: VILLAGE WOMAN
dialogue.line: Our harvest and church payments go into the abbey's accounts.

scenes.narration: Sir William Thomas Herbert of Raglan purchases the manor and lordship of Llandough and St Mary Church, bringing them into the Herbert family's territorial network.

dialogue.speaker: SIR WILLIAM THOMAS
dialogue.line: We have bought Llandough manor and added it to the Herbert estates.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL PRIEST
dialogue.line: Llandough's manorial control passes to the Herbert family of Raglan.

scenes.narration: Sir Edward Carne, a lawyer and diplomat, purchases the Llandough lordship from the 2nd Earl of Worcester, continuing high‑status lay ownership of the manor.

dialogue.speaker: SIR EDWARD CARNE
dialogue.line: I have acquired the Llandough lordship from the Earl of Worcester.

dialogue.speaker: LLANDOUGH TENANT
dialogue.line: The legal lord of Llandough changes from Worcester's line to Carne.

scenes.narration: Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries transfers Tewkesbury's ecclesiastical holdings, including Llandough lands, to the Crown as secular property.

dialogue.speaker: ROYAL COMMISSIONER
dialogue.line: These former Tewkesbury lands now vest in the Crown by statute.

dialogue.speaker: OLDER VILLAGER
dialogue.line: Control of local church lands moves from abbey to Crown authority.

scenes.narration: Post‑Dissolution grants move Llandough through lay owners and into the wider Herbert–Pembroke orbit, later feeding into what becomes the Bute estate.

dialogue.speaker: HERBERT ESTATE LAWYER
dialogue.line: Llandough is one of several manors consolidated into our estate.

dialogue.speaker: SMALLHOLDER
dialogue.line: The superior owner changes again on paper; our tenure is recorded under them.

scenes.narration: The Bute–Pembroke estate treats itself as manorial lord, issuing leases for Llandough Farm (about 166 acres) and recording long‑standing occupiers as tenants.

dialogue.speaker: MANOR STEWARD
dialogue.line: We register Llandough occupiers as tenants in the Bute–Pembroke books.

dialogue.speaker: TENANT FARMER
dialogue.line: Our occupation is recorded as a tenancy under the Bute–Pembroke estate.

scenes.narration: A Williams ancestor is admitted to Great House via the manorial court, paying a substantial entry fine remembered in family tradition as a purchase, while estate records treat it as leasehold.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS ANCESTOR
dialogue.line: I paid a large court fine to enter Great House as our family's holding.

dialogue.speaker: HERBERT STEWARD
dialogue.line: Our roll shows the Williams entry as a manorial lease, not freehold.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS ANCESTOR
dialogue.line: But this is our home now, purchased with honest coin for our heirs.

dialogue.speaker: HERBERT STEWARD
dialogue.line: The Court Baron record will show this as leasehold under our lordship.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS ANCESTOR
dialogue.line: We have the receipt. Our children will know we bought this land.

scenes.narration: Through marriage, the Llandough lordship passes into the Talbot estate at Penrice and Margam, while the Williams family continues in occupation at Great House.

dialogue.speaker: TALBOT HEIR
dialogue.line: By marriage we acquire Llandough among our Glamorgan holdings.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FAMILY MEMBER
dialogue.line: The superior lord's name changes; our occupation at Great House continues.

scenes.narration: Great House passes through elite owners, including Valentine Morris and Sir Mark Wood, before later consolidation into the Bute estate.

dialogue.speaker: VALENTINE MORRIS
dialogue.line: I treat Great House as one of several Glamorgan assets for income.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL LABOURER
dialogue.line: Estate owners change; our local work under their control continues.

scenes.narration: Sir Mark Wood acquires title and treats Great House as a revenue asset within his wider property portfolio, before it is surveyed and later taken into Bute hands.

dialogue.speaker: SIR MARK WOOD
dialogue.line: I hold Great House as an income‑producing property in my portfolio.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FARMER
dialogue.line: Our long‑term home appears in someone else's accounts as an asset.

scenes.narration: Lambert Williams of Cardiff enters formal written agreements with the Bute estate between 1818 and 1835, evidencing the Williams family as a recognised legal entity in local property dealings.

dialogue.speaker: LAMBERT WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: These written agreements show I deal with the Bute estate directly.

dialogue.speaker: BUTE ESTATE AGENT
dialogue.line: We sign deeds with Lambert Williams over Llandough premises, 1818–1835.

dialogue.speaker: LAMBERT WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: These documents record our position for future generations to cite.

scenes.narration: Chief rents of Llandough are transferred into the manorial rental accounts, simplifying estate bookkeeping and packaging obligations for future buyers.

dialogue.speaker: ESTATE ACCOUNTANT
dialogue.line: We combine Llandough chief rents into the manorial rental column.

dialogue.speaker: COTTAGER
dialogue.line: Our payments are re‑labelled on paper, but the amounts still fall on us.

scenes.narration: A land exchange between the Marquess of Bute and Lord Plymouth in Llandough consolidates Great House within Bute's controlled block of estates.

dialogue.speaker: BUTE REPRESENTATIVE
dialogue.line: This exchange secures Llandough parcels firmly within the Bute estate.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL OBSERVER
dialogue.line: New memoranda and surveys mark Bute as main landowner here.

scenes.narration: Llandough and Cogan appear in Bute rentals from 1821 onward, consolidating manorial rents under a single administrative ledger controlled by the estate.

dialogue.speaker: RENT COLLECTOR
dialogue.line: The Bute estate now logs Llandough and Cogan in the master rental.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FARMER
dialogue.line: We pay to them, though this land has been ours for generations past.

scenes.narration: Following Sir Mark Wood's property auction, surveyor David Stewart records Great House Farm under the alias 'Cedfin' in the Bute estate survey of Glamorgan holdings.

dialogue.speaker: SURVEYOR STEWART
dialogue.line: I record this property as Great House Farm, alias Cedfin, in Bute accounts.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS OCCUPANT
dialogue.line: The name on their maps matters little; we know who lives and works here.

dialogue.speaker: SURVEYOR STEWART
dialogue.line: Tithes of Llandough purchased in 1824 are now under Bute ownership.

scenes.narration: Census and tithe records shift terminology from 'Great House' to 'Great House Farm,' downgrading the property from a seat of governance to a commercial agricultural unit.

dialogue.speaker: CENSUS CLERK
dialogue.line: I enter this as Great House Farm, removing the designation of Court House.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS ELDER
dialogue.line: They rename our ancestral seat to erase our status and heritage claim.

dialogue.speaker: ESTATE LAWYER
dialogue.line: A farm designation supports our treatment of occupants as tenant farmers.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS ELDER
dialogue.line: This administrative sleight-of-hand obscures three centuries of our standing.

scenes.narration: The Williams family discovers a Roman soldier in full armor beneath the living room floor while replacing flagstones. This critical archaeological evidence is not formally recorded or disclosed.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FAMILY HEAD
dialogue.line: We've found a Roman soldier in a stone-lined grave under our floor!

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY MEMBER
dialogue.line: This proves the site is ancient and of great historical importance.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FAMILY HEAD
dialogue.line: We must tell someone—this could protect our home under the law.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL ANTIQUARIAN
dialogue.line: Fascinating find, but I doubt authorities will act on family testimony.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FAMILY HEAD
dialogue.line: One day this discovery will prove the true significance of this place.

scenes.narration: The Bute Estate carves out 33 acres from Great House Farm for Llandough Limeworks, treating the land as their own property to lease to industry, ignoring the Williams claim.

dialogue.speaker: BUTE AGENT
dialogue.line: We sever this land for the Limeworks. It's ours to lease commercially.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FARMER
dialogue.line: But we live here! You cannot carve up land we've held for two centuries.

dialogue.speaker: BUTE AGENT
dialogue.line: Estate records show no Williams ownership—only occupation under our lease.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS FARMER
dialogue.line: Our 1667 receipt and occupation prove our right to this property.

dialogue.speaker: BUTE AGENT
dialogue.line: Manorial records prevail. You are tenants, not owners, under our title.

scenes.narration: The property is systematically rebranded from 'Court House' to 'Grange' to 'Farm' in successive records, demoting occupants from gentry with tenure to mere tenant farmers.

dialogue.speaker: ESTATE CLERK
dialogue.line: We now list it simply as a farm, eliminating all reference to Court House.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS DESCENDANT
dialogue.line: This linguistic erasure strips our family of its historic manorial standing.

scenes.narration: Mary Williams is born into the family at Great House Farm, inheriting the Williams claim and continuing three centuries of unbroken occupation and assertion of ownership.

dialogue.speaker: MIDWIFE
dialogue.line: A healthy daughter! The Williams line at Great House continues.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS MATRIARCH
dialogue.line: She will know her heritage and defend this land when her time comes.

scenes.narration: Mary Williams marries Frederick Buckler but retains her maiden name, consistent with local custom and the family's understanding that the Williams lineage embodies the historic basis of title.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: I marry Frederick Buckler but keep the Williams name for our claim.

dialogue.speaker: FREDERICK BUCKLER
dialogue.line: The land belongs to your family line; the Williams name must continue.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL PRIEST
dialogue.line: Mary Williams of Great House Farm weds Frederick Buckler this day.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Our children will know they are Williams heirs to this ancestral home.

scenes.narration: The Marquess of Bute sells Great House Farm. Sale documents list it under Bute ownership, with no mention of the Williams family's three-century occupation or claim.

dialogue.speaker: BUTE ESTATE AGENT
dialogue.line: Great House Farm sells as Bute property. Occupants are sitting tenants.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: They sell our home as if we don't exist! Our family has been here since 1667.

dialogue.speaker: AUCTIONEER
dialogue.line: Estate records show clear Bute title. Occupancy doesn't equal ownership.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Where is our 1667 deed? Our family has the receipt of purchase!

dialogue.speaker: BUTE ESTATE AGENT
dialogue.line: Manorial court records supersede any claimed private family documents.

scenes.narration: The Penarth Estate Company purchases Great House Farm at auction, acquiring whatever title the Bute estate held, subject to the unresolved Williams possession and claim.

dialogue.speaker: PENARTH COMPANY DIRECTOR
dialogue.line: We purchase Great House Farm as an investment from the Bute auction.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: But you cannot buy what the Bute estate does not own! We hold this land.

dialogue.speaker: PENARTH COMPANY LAWYER
dialogue.line: Our purchase includes registered title. Your occupation will be addressed.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Three hundred years of Williams possession is not mere occupation!

scenes.narration: Despite the 1926 sale, the Williams-Buckler family remains in continuous occupation, maintaining the property and asserting their ownership against external claims.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: We stay on our land. No sale can extinguish our family's rightful claim.

dialogue.speaker: FREDERICK BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Our children work this farm and will inherit it as Williams heirs.

scenes.narration: Frederick Buckler makes the last known rent payment around 1953. From this point, the family pay nothing to any claimant, and their occupation becomes wholly adverse under limitation law.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER (YOUNG)
dialogue.line: This has been our family home for as long as anyone can remember.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: We owe rent to no one. Your grandfather secured this place for our family.

scenes.narration: Frederick Buckler's tenancy expires on 2 February 1955. Adverse possession begins unambiguously. The family attempts to register their possessory claim but lack the formal deeds the registry requires.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.line: We invite owners to register titles under the land registration system.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: I wish to register our ownership; we have occupied since 1667 and pay no rent.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.line: Do you have a deed, conveyance, or grant? Without documentary title we cannot register.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: We have family history, occupation since 1667, and our ancestor's entry receipt.

dialogue.speaker: REGISTRAR
dialogue.line: Without formal documentation we cannot register your claimed ownership.

scenes.narration: Marconi constructs a telecommunications facility adjacent to Great House Farm. Site surveys proceed without investigating the Williams ownership claim or the Roman archaeological significance.

dialogue.speaker: MARCONI SURVEYOR
dialogue.line: This site is perfect for our telecommunications base next to the farm.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Will you investigate the Roman remains we found? This is protected land.

dialogue.speaker: MARCONI OFFICIAL
dialogue.line: Our planning approval is in order. Family stories are not our concern.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: The soldier we found proves this site has archaeological importance!

dialogue.speaker: MARCONI SURVEYOR
dialogue.line: We see no official heritage listing. Development proceeds as permitted.

scenes.narration: Western Ground Rents, predecessor to BP Pension Trust, obtains the first possession order against the Bucklers on 11 December 1962 (Judge Temple Morris QC). It is never enforced due to the family's re

dialogue.speaker: COURT CLERK
dialogue.line: Possession order granted, 11 December 1962. Registered against the farmhouse and garden.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: We will not leave. This is our home. We will appeal any order they obtain.

dialogue.speaker: RECORDS CLERK
dialogue.line: The landlord holds the order but has not yet moved to enforce it.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: We file a defence based on adverse possession under the Limitation Act 1939.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Our family has been here since 1667. No court order can make us leave.

scenes.narration: Mary Williams consults solicitors. Legal advice confirms the 1962 possession order was never enforced, the Limitation Act may have run in the family's favour, but court proceedings are essential to es

dialogue.speaker: SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Your family's continuous possession since 1667 supports adverse possession.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Then we can prove ownership and settle this once and for all?

dialogue.speaker: SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: The 1962 order exists but was not enforced. A court must rule on adverse possession.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: What if they refuse to rule on ownership and only address possession?

dialogue.speaker: SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Ownership is the only issue that can conclusively settle this dispute.

scenes.narration: BP Pension Trust Ltd applies to enforce the 1962 possession order. Mary files a defence asserting adverse possession. On 31 October 1974, BP Pension Trust issues unilateral licence letters to Mrs Buck

dialogue.speaker: COURT CLERK
dialogue.line: BP Pension Trust applies to enforce the 1962 possession order forthwith.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS' SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: We file a defence: the landlord's title has been extinguished by adverse possession since 1955.

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: Warrant to issue but not be enforced until 31 October 1974 pending appeal.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: We received a letter offering us a licence to stay rent-free. We never agreed to that.

dialogue.speaker: COURT CLERK
dialogue.line: BP Pension Trust's October 1974 licence letter is now on the court record.

scenes.narration: The estate interest is transferred by the head of the title chain. Mary Williams argues the sale cannot extinguish her adverse possession claim, which was asserted on record the previous year.

dialogue.speaker: ESTATE AGENT
dialogue.line: The superior title passes to new holders. Sitting occupants are noted in the file.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: You cannot sell what you do not own! My court case is still pending!

dialogue.speaker: ESTATE AGENT
dialogue.line: Our registered title permits this transaction despite the pending occupants' claim.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Adjourned means unresolved—not dismissed! Our adverse possession defence stands!

scenes.narration: New claimants demand rent. The Williams-Buckler family refuses, asserting continuous adverse possession since at least 1955, while owners rely on the unenforced 1962 order and the 1974 licence letter.

dialogue.speaker: NEW OWNER'S AGENT
dialogue.line: You must pay rent or vacate. We hold title to this property.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: We own this farm! Our family has been here for over three centuries!

dialogue.speaker: NEW OWNER'S AGENT
dialogue.line: Registered title is conclusive. Your occupation is without legal right.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Our continuous possession creates title! You've never proven you own it!

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: The court has not ruled. Until ownership is determined, we stay.

scenes.narration: Legal proceedings commence to determine possession, but again ownership is not adjudicated. The court focuses on narrow possession questions without resolving the fundamental ownership dispute.

dialogue.speaker: OPPOSING COUNSEL
dialogue.line: We seek possession based on our client's registered title to the property.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Respectfully, ownership must be determined first before possession can be ruled.

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: This court will determine possession. Ownership is a separate matter.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: But possession flows from ownership! How can you rule on one without the other?

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: We proceed on the possession claim. The ownership issue is not before us.

scenes.narration: A small rescue excavation near Great House uncovers Roman remains, confirming archaeological significance, but the full extent is not disclosed and development pressures continue.

dialogue.speaker: ARCHAEOLOGIST
dialogue.line: We've found Roman artifacts confirming the Williams family's 1870 discovery.

dialogue.speaker: PLANNING OFFICER
dialogue.line: This is a limited dig. We've no basis for full site protection at this time.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: This proves our home sits on a major historical site! It must be protected!

dialogue.speaker: PLANNING OFFICER
dialogue.line: Unless Cadw formally lists it, development can proceed subject to conditions.

dialogue.speaker: ARCHAEOLOGIST
dialogue.line: The full extent of remains likely won't be known until after demolition.

scenes.narration: Possession proceedings drag on. The family argues that without determining ownership, any possession order is premature and procedurally unsafe, but their objection is not addressed.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: You cannot lawfully determine possession without first establishing ownership!

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: The claim before us is for possession, not a declaration of ownership.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: But if they don't own it, they can't claim possession from us!

dialogue.speaker: OPPOSING COUNSEL
dialogue.line: Our client has registered title. That is sufficient for this possession claim.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Registered title is not proof of ownership if obtained through defective process!

scenes.narration: BP Properties Ltd is registered as proprietor of Great House Farm in November 1982, taking whatever title the chain provided. Mary Williams (Mrs Buckler) is still alive and in residence at the time of

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES LAWYER
dialogue.line: We are registered as proprietor of Great House Farm from November 1982.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: Another transfer! They keep selling our home while our adverse possession claim stands!

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES LAWYER
dialogue.line: Our title is registered. The 1974 licence letter means your claim is not adverse.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: How can you be bona fide when our possession and claim are fully on record?

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES LAWYER
dialogue.line: We acquired from the registered proprietor. Your claim is against the prior vendor.

scenes.narration: Mary Williams (Mrs Buckler) dies in 1983. Billy Buckler junior must now claim through her estate. The 1667 deed and later conveyances remain missing, preventing documentary proof of the family's posse

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: The 1667 deed and manorial records that would prove your claim are missing.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: My mother is gone. Where are the documents she always said we had?

dialogue.speaker: ARCHIVE CLERK
dialogue.line: We have no record of any Williams conveyance in the Bute estate archives.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Convenient that every document proving our ownership has vanished!

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Missing deeds raise serious questions. Billy must now claim through her estate.

scenes.narration: BP Properties asserts title and relies on the 1974 licence letters issued by BP Pension Trust, its predecessor. The family never accepted or rejected those letters, and BP Properties now uses them to

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES AGENT
dialogue.line: We hold registered title and rely on the 1974 licence letters sent to Mrs Buckler.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Those letters were sent by BP Pension Trust in 1974—before you even owned this land!

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES AGENT
dialogue.line: We acquired the benefit of those letters as successors in title to BP Pension Trust.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: My mother never accepted that licence. She disputed it until she died in 1983!

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES AGENT
dialogue.line: She never rejected it in writing. The licence stands under BP Properties Ltd v Buckler.

scenes.narration: Proceedings before Hollis J in the Queen's Bench Division at Cardiff examine the adverse possession claim and the legal effect of the 1974 licence letters. The identity substitution from Mary Williams

dialogue.speaker: OPPOSING COUNSEL
dialogue.line: Our client relies on the 1974 licence granting Mrs Buckler rent-free occupation for life.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Mary Williams never accepted that licence and contested the name Mrs Buckler!

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: The licence document refers to Mrs Buckler. Is that the same person as Mary Williams?

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: I am Mary Williams! I never accepted the name Buckler on any legal document!

dialogue.speaker: OPPOSING COUNSEL
dialogue.line: Mary Williams married Frederick Buckler. Mrs Buckler is her legal married name.

scenes.narration: The family raises the 1870 Roman soldier discovery and requests Cadw investigate before any demolition, but officials say they need formal application and supporting evidence to list.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: We found a Roman soldier here in 1870! This site must be protected!

dialogue.speaker: CADW OFFICER
dialogue.line: Do you have archaeological reports or documentation of the discovery?

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: It was our family's discovery! This proves the site's national importance!

dialogue.speaker: CADW OFFICER
dialogue.line: Without documented evidence, we cannot proceed with emergency listing.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: So family testimony of archaeological finds is ignored until it's too late?

scenes.narration: Hollis J gives judgment on 24 July 1986 in the Queen's Bench Division at Cardiff, ruling against the Bucklers. Fraud and identity-substitution allegations are noted but no investigation is ordered.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: We allege fraud in the procurement of title and deliberate document suppression.

dialogue.speaker: OPPOSING COUNSEL
dialogue.line: These are serious allegations without proof. Our client's title is registered.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: The missing 1667 deed and identity substitution demand investigation!

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: Your fraud allegations are noted, but this court's task is the adverse possession point.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Under Takhar v Gracefield, fraud unravels all—but only if investigated!

scenes.narration: Following the Queen's Bench judgment, BP Properties applies for planning permission to demolish Great House Farm. The application proceeds without disclosing the Roman burial or the pending appeal.

dialogue.speaker: PLANNING OFFICER
dialogue.line: BP Properties seeks permission to demolish and redevelop Great House Farm.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: What about the family's claim? And the archaeological significance?

dialogue.speaker: PLANNING OFFICER
dialogue.line: The ownership dispute is civil law. We assess the planning merits only.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: You can't permit demolition when ownership is contested and Roman remains exist!

dialogue.speaker: PLANNING OFFICER
dialogue.line: Without official heritage listing, we cannot refuse based on archaeology.

scenes.narration: The Court of Appeal (Dillon LJ) delivers judgment on 31 July 1987 in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler. The appeal is dismissed. The 1974 unilateral licence letter ended adverse possession without need for

dialogue.speaker: DILLON LJ
dialogue.line: The unilateral 1974 licence letter ended adverse possession regardless of acceptance.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY BARRISTER
dialogue.line: My Lords—m'Lord—the licence was never accepted. Adverse possession must have continued!

dialogue.speaker: DILLON LJ
dialogue.line: Adverse possession ceased from receipt of the letters. BP Pension Trust's title revived.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY BARRISTER
dialogue.line: The licence substituted Mrs Buckler for Mary Williams without consent or explanation!

dialogue.speaker: DILLON LJ
dialogue.line: Appeal dismissed. BP Properties Ltd is entitled to possession of the farm.

scenes.narration: After the Court of Appeal ruling, family members reveal that Frederick Buckler had negotiated or settled legal matters prior to his death without informing the family, causing a lasting rift.

dialogue.speaker: DAVID BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Dad said Grandad Frederick 'sorted it legally' before he died in secret.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: What did he sort? He never told us what he signed or agreed to!

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: I never authorised any settlement. I am the Williams heir, not Frederick!

dialogue.speaker: DAVID BUCKLER
dialogue.line: That secrecy caused a rift and left us unsure what rights were signed away.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: If Grandad secretly dealt away our inheritance, that's another fraud!

scenes.narration: Following the Court of Appeal ruling, the family explores an application to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 1 Protocol 1, but face the argument that domestic remedies are not exhauste

dialogue.speaker: EUROPEAN RIGHTS LAWYER
dialogue.line: You have grounds for an Article 1 Protocol 1 claim on property deprivation.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Finally, a court that might examine what UK courts refused to address!

dialogue.speaker: GOVERNMENT SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Domestic remedies have not been exhausted. The application is premature.

dialogue.speaker: EUROPEAN RIGHTS LAWYER
dialogue.line: Every UK court refused to determine ownership! What remedy remains?

dialogue.speaker: GOVERNMENT SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Procedural rules bar this application. Domestic courts have ruled conclusively.

scenes.narration: BP Properties presses for immediate possession. The family refuses to vacate, asserting ownership was never proven and warning that demolition will destroy irreplaceable heritage and evidence.

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES AGENT
dialogue.line: You must vacate immediately. The court has granted us possession.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Possession was granted, but ownership was never proven in any court!

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES AGENT
dialogue.line: The Court of Appeal has ruled. Further resistance is contempt of court.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: This house is over 800 years old! Demolition destroys our heritage forever!

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: And it destroys the Roman site underneath! This is deliberate evidence destruction!

scenes.narration: Bailiffs arrive to enforce possession, but the family resists, barricading themselves inside Great House Farm and refusing to leave without a ruling on ownership and heritage protection.

dialogue.speaker: BAILIFF
dialogue.line: We are here to enforce the court order for possession. Open the door.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Not until ownership is proven and this site's archaeology is protected!

dialogue.speaker: BAILIFF
dialogue.line: You are in contempt of court. Police assistance will be requested.

dialogue.speaker: MARY WILLIAMS
dialogue.line: We are the rightful owners! This eviction is based on fraud and deceit!

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Demolish this house and you destroy evidence of national importance!

scenes.narration: A tense standoff ensues. Bailiffs, police, and media surround Great House Farm. Inside, the Williams-Buckler family vows to resist until ownership is judicially determined and heritage protected.

dialogue.speaker: POLICE COMMANDER
dialogue.line: This situation must be resolved peacefully. Will you exit voluntarily?

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Only if the court determines ownership and Cadw protects this site!

dialogue.speaker: MEDIA REPORTER
dialogue.line: Why has ownership never been ruled on in over a decade of litigation?

dialogue.speaker: POLICE COMMANDER
dialogue.line: Our role is enforcement, not adjudication. The courts have ruled.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: The courts ruled on possession, not ownership! That's the entire point!

scenes.narration: Police storm Great House Farm. Billy Buckler is injured and hospitalized during the forcible eviction. The family, including pregnant Branwen and young children, are removed by force.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: You have no right! This is our home! Ownership was never proven!

dialogue.speaker: POLICE OFFICER
dialogue.line: We are enforcing a court order. Resisting will result in arrest.

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Please! I am pregnant and we have small children! Where will we go?

dialogue.speaker: POLICE OFFICER
dialogue.line: Social services will assist. You must vacate immediately.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: This is state-sanctioned theft! Our family has been here for 321 years!

scenes.narration: Billy Buckler is hospitalised with injuries from the forcible eviction. His pregnant wife Branwen and young children are homeless. All possessions remain sealed inside the empty farmhouse.

dialogue.speaker: NURSE
dialogue.line: You have significant injuries from the eviction. You need to rest here.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: I need to get back to protect my home and my family's possessions!

dialogue.speaker: DOCTOR
dialogue.line: You're in no condition to leave. The police have barred you from the site.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: What about my pregnant wife and children? Where are they sleeping tonight?

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Billy is in hospital. I have the children and another on the way and nowhere to go.

scenes.narration: Branwen and the children stay with relatives. The family's belongings, farm equipment, and Mary Williams' journal documenting visitors and events are sealed inside Great House.

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: We're sleeping in my sister's front room with three children and one on the way.

dialogue.speaker: RELATIVE
dialogue.line: You can stay as long as needed, but what will happen to your things?

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Nan's journal was inside. Names, dates, all the visitors—now locked away.

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Everything is locked inside—furniture, clothes, equipment, Nan's journal.

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: They've taken our home and trapped our proof inside with it.

scenes.narration: The family's lawyers seek an emergency injunction to halt demolition pending heritage review and investigation of fraud allegations, but face procedural obstacles and time pressure.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: We need an emergency injunction to stop demolition until Cadw investigates.

dialogue.speaker: COURT CLERK
dialogue.line: You must demonstrate irreparable harm and good grounds for the injunction.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Demolition destroys an 800-year-old building and a Roman archaeological site!

dialogue.speaker: COURT CLERK
dialogue.line: Is the building listed? Has Cadw granted statutory protection?

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Not yet, but we've applied! Demolition before listing would be irreversible!

scenes.narration: A temporary injunction is granted, halting demolition for a brief period while Cadw considers emergency listing and the family's appeal attempts proceed through legal channels.

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: I grant a temporary injunction against demolition pending further hearing.

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES LAWYER
dialogue.line: This injunction frustrates our lawful rights following the Court of Appeal ruling!

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Heritage protection and fraud allegations must be examined before demolition!

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: The injunction is limited in time. Cadw must decide on listing promptly.

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES LAWYER
dialogue.line: Every delay costs our client money and undermines the finality of judgments.

scenes.narration: Cadw conducts a rushed assessment of Great House Farm for emergency listing, but pressure from BP Properties and lack of accessible documentation impede the evaluation process.

dialogue.speaker: CADW INSPECTOR
dialogue.line: We need detailed architectural and historical evidence for listing.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: The house is 800 years old and sits on a Roman burial site!

dialogue.speaker: CADW INSPECTOR
dialogue.line: Can you provide structural surveys, historical documentation, archaeological reports?

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: All our family records were sealed inside when they evicted us!

dialogue.speaker: CADW INSPECTOR
dialogue.line: Without supporting documentation, emergency listing is difficult to justify.

scenes.narration: The family appeals to the media and public, explaining that ownership was never determined, archaeological evidence was suppressed, and heritage protection has been denied.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Since 1974, no court has ever ruled who actually owns this property!

dialogue.speaker: JOURNALIST
dialogue.line: Why not? Isn't ownership the fundamental question in a possession case?

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Exactly! They avoided that because our 321 years of possession proves ownership!

dialogue.speaker: JOURNALIST
dialogue.line: What about the archaeological finds your family discovered?

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Ignored until it's convenient to dig up what's left after they destroy the house!

scenes.narration: Local residents and councillors express outrage at the eviction and planned demolition, condemning BP Properties for destroying heritage and the authorities for enabling it.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: This eviction and demolition plan is a travesty of justice!

dialogue.speaker: COMMUNITY MEMBER
dialogue.line: How can they demolish an 800-year-old building on a Roman burial ground?

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: We've demanded BP halt demolition and the council refuse planning permission!

dialogue.speaker: PLANNING OFFICER
dialogue.line: The council has limited powers once court possession orders are granted.

dialogue.speaker: COMMUNITY MEMBER
dialogue.line: So corporate interests override heritage, history, and a family's 321-year claim?

scenes.narration: Cardiff MP Alun Michael asks the Lord Chancellor to review the case, highlighting the failure to determine ownership and the procedural anomalies throughout the litigation.

dialogue.speaker: ALUN MICHAEL MP
dialogue.line: Lord Chancellor, this case shows serious procedural failures and injustice.

dialogue.speaker: LORD CHANCELLOR'S AIDE
dialogue.line: The courts have ruled at the highest level. What grounds justify review?

dialogue.speaker: ALUN MICHAEL MP
dialogue.line: Ownership was never determined! That's a fundamental defect in every ruling!

dialogue.speaker: LORD CHANCELLOR'S AIDE
dialogue.line: The House of Lords addressed the possession claim comprehensively.

dialogue.speaker: ALUN MICHAEL MP
dialogue.line: But possession without ownership determination is procedurally unsafe and unjust!

scenes.narration: As days pass, the temporary injunction approaches expiry. Cadw has not granted emergency listing. BP Properties presses for the injunction to be lifted and demolition to proceed.

dialogue.speaker: CADW SPOKESPERSON
dialogue.line: We are considering, but have not granted, emergency listing for Great House.

dialogue.speaker: JANET HARRIS (BUCKLER)
dialogue.line: This very old house still has no legal protection against demolition.

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES LAWYER
dialogue.line: The injunction must be lifted. Our client has been unlawfully delayed.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: If demolition proceeds before listing, heritage is lost forever!

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES LAWYER
dialogue.line: Speculation about heritage cannot indefinitely frustrate lawful property rights.

scenes.narration: A judge refuses to extend the injunction. Cadw declines emergency listing. Demolition is cleared to proceed with registered title upheld and no investigation of fraud or missing deeds.

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: There is no sufficient legal basis to continue the demolition injunction.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: But the archaeology and fraud allegations remain uninvestigated!

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: Those matters do not support further delay of lawful possession and use.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY SOLICITOR
dialogue.line: Once the house is demolished, European Court review cannot restore it!

dialogue.speaker: JANET HARRIS (BUCKLER)
dialogue.line: Without listing, they're now free to demolish the building immediately.

scenes.narration: On 6 December 1988, Great House Farm is demolished overnight, hours after the final court decision, ending over three centuries of Williams-Buckler occupation and destroying the structure.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: The farmhouse has been demolished overnight after the court ruling.

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: We watched from the caravan as the house was taken down to rubble.

dialogue.speaker: DEMOLITION FOREMAN
dialogue.line: We carried out demolition as instructed once legal clearance was given.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL OBSERVER
dialogue.line: They demolished it immediately—no delay for appeals or heritage review.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: They destroyed our home and all the evidence inside before anyone could act!

scenes.narration: Shortly after demolition and eviction, police take Billy from his hospital bed to face charges of assaulting two bailiffs during the enforcement action at Great House Farm.

dialogue.speaker: POLICE OFFICER
dialogue.line: You are under arrest for assaults alleged during the eviction process.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: I am being brought from hospital to answer charges tied to the eviction.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: I was defending my family's home from an unlawful eviction!

dialogue.speaker: POLICE OFFICER
dialogue.line: The eviction was court-ordered. Resistance constitutes assault and contempt.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: How can it be lawful when ownership was never proven in any court?

scenes.narration: Officials report that the cleared farm site resembles a battleground. The local authority begins legal steps to require BP Properties to remove debris and restore basic order.

dialogue.speaker: PLANNING CHIEF
dialogue.line: The condition of the site is unacceptable; we will seek enforcement.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: We intend to require BP to clear rubble and restore basic order.

dialogue.speaker: VALE COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: We regard BP's complete flattening of the site as wholly unjustified.

dialogue.speaker: BP PROPERTIES AGENT
dialogue.line: We demolished our own property lawfully. Cleanup is underway.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: This destruction of heritage and a family's home is a disgrace!

scenes.narration: After losing the farmhouse and contents, the family live in temporary and borrowed accommodation. Billy estimates their lost belongings and livelihood at roughly thirty thousand pounds.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: After eviction I have no house, stock, or equipment left to rely on.

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: We are staying with family members while we have three children and one due.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: I estimate our lost property and livelihood at about thirty thousand pounds.

dialogue.speaker: BRANWEN BUCKLER
dialogue.line: They've taken everything—our home, our history, our future.

scenes.narration: A threatening-behaviour charge against Billy is withdrawn as out of time. Assault and driving allegations from the eviction events continue, and exclusion conditions remain in place.

dialogue.speaker: PROSECUTOR CLARKE
dialogue.line: We withdraw the threatening-behaviour count as the summons is late.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Even so, I am still barred from going near the former farm site.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: They evict us by force, then prosecute me for resisting their violence!

dialogue.speaker: PROSECUTOR CLARKE
dialogue.line: The court order was lawful. Your resistance constituted criminal conduct.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Nothing about this was lawful! Ownership was never proven!

scenes.narration: Billy pleads guilty to remaining charges and is freed, stating that he will continue to contest the loss of the family home and land despite the completed demolition.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: I will go on challenging how our home and the land were taken from us.

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: The matter is concluded. The property has been demolished.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Demolished, yes—but the fraud, the missing deeds, the suppressed archaeology remain!

dialogue.speaker: JUDGE
dialogue.line: Those are civil matters beyond this court's criminal jurisdiction.

dialogue.speaker: BILLY BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Justice demands investigation! Someone must examine what happened here!

scenes.narration: Site clearance in March removes remaining physical traces. Lorries export rubble over several days, leaving little to show future residents the contested history beneath.

dialogue.speaker: SITE MANAGER
dialogue.line: Our job is simple: remove all remnants so the site is ready for housing.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL HISTORIAN
dialogue.line: They're erasing the last physical evidence of what happened here.

dialogue.speaker: SITE MANAGER
dialogue.line: We follow orders. The site must be cleared for redevelopment.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL HISTORIAN
dialogue.line: Rubble removal completes the destruction—house, history, heritage, gone.

scenes.narration: At a village meeting, residents condemn the demolition and seek ways to stop BP Properties profiting from redevelopment, but are told legal avenues to reverse or claw back are minimal.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL ACTIVIST
dialogue.line: They used planning and courts to clear obstacles; now profit is the goal.

dialogue.speaker: COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: Without title or listing on your side, leverage over BP is almost gone.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL ACTIVIST
dialogue.line: Is there no mechanism to challenge a demolition achieved through suspected fraud?

dialogue.speaker: COUNCILLOR
dialogue.line: Fraud allegations require proof and investigation—neither has occurred.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL ACTIVIST
dialogue.line: So BP demolishes under disputed title and profits while the family suffers?

scenes.narration: Press coverage moves on, presenting the case as finished: family out, house gone, site in BP's hands. Unresolved questions about missing deeds, licences, and adverse possession fade from public view.

dialogue.speaker: NEWSPAPER EDITOR
dialogue.line: With no new hearings, we treat this as a closed eviction and demolition story.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL HISTORIAN
dialogue.line: Key gaps—lost deeds, licence letters, estate records—remain unexplored.

dialogue.speaker: NEWSPAPER EDITOR
dialogue.line: Without new evidence or proceedings, there's no story to sustain coverage.

dialogue.speaker: LOCAL HISTORIAN
dialogue.line: The story is the unanswered questions! Ownership never determined, fraud uninvestigated!

dialogue.speaker: NEWSPAPER EDITOR
dialogue.line: Public interest has moved on. The site is being redeveloped.

scenes.narration: Major excavation at the former farm site uncovers a Roman villa and over eight hundred burials, confirming the land's national archaeological importance after the house is demolished.

dialogue.speaker: LEAD ARCHAEOLOGIST
dialogue.line: These burials and villa remains show this was a site of national importance.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS DESCENDANT
dialogue.line: Our family's 1870 Roman-soldier account is confirmed only after demolition.

dialogue.speaker: ARCHAEOLOGIST
dialogue.line: Earlier recognition of this evidence could have triggered protection laws.

dialogue.speaker: WILLIAMS DESCENDANT
dialogue.line: They ignored our testimony, demolished the house, then 'discovered' what we told them!

dialogue.speaker: LEAD ARCHAEOLOGIST
dialogue.line: This is one of the largest burial grounds ever excavated in Wales.

scenes.narration: Heritage publications celebrate the Llandough archaeology but omit the eviction and demolition story. Modern residents live over the site unaware of the recent dispossession.

dialogue.speaker: HERITAGE EDITOR
dialogue.line: We present the villa and burials as a heritage success, not an eviction site.

dialogue.speaker: MODERN RESIDENT
dialogue.line: I learned of Roman remains here, not of a family being removed.

dialogue.speaker: HERITAGE EDITOR
dialogue.line: The archaeology is the story we tell—the human cost is not our focus.

dialogue.speaker: MODERN RESIDENT
dialogue.line: So the history is sanitized? The Bucklers erased from the site's narrative?

dialogue.speaker: HERITAGE EDITOR
dialogue.line: Our remit is archaeological heritage, not contemporary property disputes.

scenes.narration: Family accounts suggest Frederick Buckler may have secretly settled or sold interests before 1987, contributing to internal rupture and confusion over what was legally agreed.

dialogue.speaker: DAVID BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Dad said Grandad 'sorted it legally' when he sold, but never explained how.

dialogue.speaker: DAVID BUCKLER
dialogue.line: That secrecy caused a rift and left us unsure what rights were signed away.

dialogue.speaker: DAVID BUCKLER
dialogue.line: Nan's journal, naming visitors and dates, was lost with the farmhouse.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY MEMBER
dialogue.line: If Grandad settled secretly, did that undermine Nan's ownership claim?

dialogue.speaker: DAVID BUCKLER
dialogue.line: We don't know! The documents and Nan's journal were destroyed with the house!

scenes.narration: Relatives assert Rhys Buckler's position as heir to manorial rights through the Williams-Buckler line. His disability raises questions about equal treatment of vulnerable heirs in the legal process.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY ADVOCATE
dialogue.line: Rhys's claim should be assessed on law, not quietly sidelined by disability.

dialogue.speaker: CONTEMPORARY LAWYER
dialogue.line: Courts favour written, registered rights; oral and equitable claims struggle.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY ADVOCATE
dialogue.line: But three centuries of continuous possession by the Williams-Buckler line created rights!

dialogue.speaker: CONTEMPORARY LAWYER
dialogue.line: Adverse possession claims require court determination—which never occurred.

dialogue.speaker: FAMILY ADVOCATE
dialogue.line: Exactly—ownership was never adjudicated! The case remains unresolved!

scenes.narration: Church View Close now covers the site of Great House Farm, the Marconi base, and one of Wales's largest recorded burial excavations, yet no plaque or record notes the clearance or dispute.

dialogue.speaker: RESIDENT'S CHILD
dialogue.line: Dad, I want to build a radio and plant a tree and own this house we live in.

dialogue.speaker: FATHER
dialogue.line: Don't think that way or say that out loud, son. It brings us big trouble here.

dialogue.speaker: RESIDENT'S CHILD
dialogue.line: But why?

dialogue.speaker: FATHER
dialogue.line: The last family to speak like that are traumatised into silence, three decades later.

dialogue.speaker: RESIDENT'S CHILD
dialogue.line: Well, I will speak up. And for them too.

scenes.narration: Modern researchers examining the case identify a pattern: ownership never adjudicated, documents missing, archaeology suppressed, identity substituted between Mary Williams and Mrs Buckler, fraud unin

dialogue.speaker: LEGAL RESEARCHER
dialogue.line: Every court avoided the ownership question—the only issue that mattered.

dialogue.speaker: HISTORIAN
dialogue.line: The 1667 deed, manorial records, Mary Williams' journal—all missing or destroyed.

dialogue.speaker: LEGAL RESEARCHER
dialogue.line: The Roman burial was reported in 1870 but ignored until post-demolition excavation.

dialogue.speaker: HISTORIAN
dialogue.line: Mary Williams became Mrs Buckler in legal documents without explanation or consent.

dialogue.speaker: LEGAL RESEARCHER
dialogue.line: Under Takhar v Gracefield, fraud unravels all—but only if investigated.

scenes.narration: Legal scholars note the case exemplifies how procedural avoidance, missing documentation, and rushed demolition can circumvent substantive justice and heritage protection.

dialogue.speaker: LAW PROFESSOR
dialogue.line: This case shows how possession can be determined without addressing ownership.

dialogue.speaker: HERITAGE EXPERT
dialogue.line: Demolition before listing creates irreversible loss of heritage and evidence.

dialogue.speaker: LAW PROFESSOR
dialogue.line: The Williams-Buckler family asserted ownership for 321 years without force or secrecy.

dialogue.speaker: HERITAGE EXPERT
dialogue.line: While corporate claimants operated through licence, substitution, and stealth.

dialogue.speaker: LAW PROFESSOR
dialogue.line: Justice requires investigation: who owned it? Where are the deeds? Why the rush?

scenes.narration: Advocates call for a public inquiry to examine the combined effect of procedural avoidance, identity substitution, heritage omission, and irreversible consequence in the Great House Farm case.

dialogue.speaker: ADVOCATE
dialogue.line: No public inquiry has examined how this dispossession was achieved.

dialogue.speaker: PARLIAMENTARIAN
dialogue.line: What remedy exists when courts avoid ownership and demolition destroys evidence?

dialogue.speaker: ADVOCATE
dialogue.line: Declaratory justice: determine who owned it, correct the record, recognise the Williams-Buckler clai

dialogue.speaker: PARLIAMENTARIAN
dialogue.line: And if fraud is established, what compensation is owed?

dialogue.speaker: ADVOCATE
dialogue.line: Preliminarily quantified at approximately £101.2 million, but truth comes first.

timeline.event: Robert Fitzhamon grants Llandough lordship to Walsche family
Construction of Tŷ Mawr (Great House) begins
Herbert family acquires Llandough manor
Sir Edward Carne purchases Llandough lordship
Dissolution of the Monasteries transfers lands to Crown
Williams ancestor enters Great House via manorial court
Talbot estate acquires Llandough through marriage
Great House recorded as 'Cedfin' in Bute survey
Roman soldier discovered beneath living room floor
Bute Estate seizes 33 acres for Limeworks
Mary Williams born at Great House Farm
Mary Williams marries Frederick Buckler
Marquess of Bute sells Great House Farm
Frederick Buckler makes last rent payment; adverse possession begins approximately 1953
Land registration laws enacted; Williams claim not registered
Marconi constructs telecommunications facility
First possession order obtained by Western Ground Rents (Judge Temple Morris QC, 11 Dec 1962)
BP Pension Trust enforces 1962 order; unilateral licence letters issued to Mrs Buckler
Penarth Estate sells to new buyers despite pending case
BP Properties acquires Great House Farm
Mary Williams (Mrs Buckler) dies; Billy Buckler junior must claim through her estate
Hollis J (QBD Cardiff) rules against Bucklers on 24 July 1986
Court of Appeal rules in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (31 July 1987)
Great House Farm demolished (December 6)
Major excavation confirms Roman villa and 800+ burials

legalCases.outcome: Possession granted to BP Properties; adverse possession claim failed due to unilateral licence
legalCases.significance: Court of Appeal (Dillon LJ) held the 1974 unilateral licence letter ended adverse possession without acceptance; possession granted to BP Properties

legalCases.outcome: No reasonable diligence requirement to set aside judgment obtained by fraud
legalCases.significance: Referenced in screenplay: 'fraud unravels all—but only if investigated'
